# msknockoffs

<!-- badges: start -->
<!-- badges: end -->

msknockoffs stands for multi-study knockoffs. This package helps to get a set of variables that are associated with a response $y$. The package contains a main algorithm that is able to use $K$ datasets of gene expression data. It calculates knockoffs from two methods (sequential and second-order), $Z$ and $Z$-knockoff statistics of the $K$ datasets, creates a combination of all knockoffs with help of OSFF function, calculates $W$ statistics and the threshold, and finally returns a selection of variables.

## Installation

You can install the development version of msknockoffs like so:

``` r
# install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("lisandrobles/msknockoffs")
```

## Use of the X-model of knockoffs for the identification of cancer diagnostic genes from considering lung gene expression data from multiple sources.

This example illustrates the main function. We are using three datasets that contain gene expression information related to lung cancer. The objective of this example is to show that this algorithm can obtain a set of variables, and identifying these variables helps us understand which gene expressions are most associated with lung cancerous tissue; furthermore, it also allows us to create a classification model between healthy and tumorous tissue. Also this algorithm can control FDR.

First load the necessary libraries:

```{r example}
#install.packages("knockoff")
library(knockoff)
#devtools::install_github("kormama1/seqknockoff")
library(seqknockoff)
#install.packages("glmnet")
library(glmnet)
#install.packages("clustermq")
library(clustermq)
#devtools::install_github("lisandrobles/msknockoffs")
library(msknockoffs)
```

Getting the data ready

```{r}
data1 <- read.csv("data/18_Lu_2010_100.csv",header = TRUE)
data2 <- read.csv("data/36_Selamat_2012_100.csv",header = TRUE)
data3 <- read.csv("data/2_Landi_2008_100.csv",header = TRUE)
```

Here we need to set out the parameters that the main function needs. In the R console write ?selection to see this function documentation and usage.

```{r}
Xlist <- list(data1[,-c(1)],data2[,-c(1)],data3[,-c(1)])
Ylist <- list(data1$Sam_Tissue,data2$Sam_Tissue,data3$Sam_Tissue)
familylist=c("binomial","binomial","binomial")
Kmethod=c("second","second","second")
Zmethod=c("glmnet","glmnet","glmnet")
Wmethod="D_Max_Sum"
q = 0.2
offset = 1
```
This algorithm is very flexible, you can use the number of dataset you like, select different methods for calculating knockoffs, diferent W functions, etc.

Then we call the main function. This function calculates knockoffs, Z and Z-knockoff statistics, creates a combination of all knockoffs, and calculates W statistics and the threshold. Finally, it returns a selection of variables.

```{r}
selection_of_indices <- selection(Xlist,Ylist,familylist,Kmethod,Zmethod,q,offset,Wmethod)
```

The function gene_id() is very useful to get the name id of indices.

```{r}
gene_id_selection <- gene_id(selection_of_indices,q,data1)
```
This indices can be found and study in web page from USA goverment, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/.

Another important function in this package is the function that can make a number of $n$ selections, that is, yo can run for example fifty times the function an the using a rule propose in Kormaksson et al., 2021, get a final set of indices or variables. This make the selection more robust.

```{r warning=FALSE}
n_selection_of_indices <- n_selection(n=50,Xlist,Ylist,familylist,Kmethod,Zmethod,q,offset,Wmethod)
```

Using the gene_id function

```{r}
n_gene_id_selection <- gene_id(n_selection_of_indices,q,data1)
```
It may seem that doing a lot selection gives fewer selected indices; the reason is that with this form of selection, the FDR is totally controlled.
